Estimate which month the snapshot describes. Use only the figures supplied plus your general knowledge of economic history.

text:
This looks like April 2009. Equities rebounded sharply over the month (US large-cap +13.4%, emerging markets +24.4%), which fits a market bottoming in March 2009 and rallying into April. The 12-month drawdown of about -43% also fits.

The macro figures point the same way. Unemployment is 8.1%, which matches the February 2009 reading, and the fed funds rate is near zero. Payrolls are averaging about -660k a month, consistent with early 2009. Headline CPI at roughly 0% YoY fits March 2009, which was about -0.4%, while February was +0.2%.

That leaves the choice between March and April. If the month were March 2009, the S&P 500 1-month return would be about +8.5%. The S&P 500 rose from 735 at the end of February to 797 at the end of March, then to 872 at the end of April, so a +13.4% month does not match March for US large-caps. Emerging markets rose about 24% in the month, which is closer to the March 9 to April run. The 3-month return of -7.8% fits end-March better: from end-December 2008 (903) to end-March (797) is about -11.7%, or about -8% with dividends and some difference in the index. April's 3-month return, from end-January (825) to end-April (872), would be positive, so April does not fit.

The reported unemployment of 8.1% matches February 2009, and the data available at the end of March would show the February figure. Headline CPI of +0.07 fits February's +0.2% reading less well, but the figure could be a rounded or revised value. The 10-year yield at 2.73% is also lower than the end-March level of about 2.67%.

The 1-month +13.4% for US equities is hard to square with March. However, a lag in the data could explain it, and the month is most likely March 2009 on the other evidence.
